profile.summary: RhoMax predicts the wavelength of light a microbial rhodopsin absorbs most strongly, from its amino acid sequence alone. The sequence is first folded by AlphaFold2, then the 24 residues that line the retinal binding pocket are cut out and turned into a graph: one node per atom, an edge between atoms within 2 Angstrom. A small graph neural network reads that graph and returns one number, the absorption maximum in nanometres. The purpose is to find red-shifted rhodopsins for optogenetics without measuring each candidate.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The sequence is folded with AlphaFold2, run with default parameters and without templates, and the highest-ranked model is kept; the authors measure a median RMSD of 1.08 Angstrom against the crystal structures they could check. A multiple sequence alignment picks out the 24 binding pocket residues. Each atom of those residues becomes a node with a feature vector of spatial and chemical properties, and atoms within 2 Angstrom are joined by an edge whose features come from the distance. The network is four graph layers: graph convolution, two graph attention layers, then graph convolution, each without self-loops and with one attention head, followed by batch normalisation and an ELU activation, with mean aggregation at the end to give a single number. It is designed to be invariant to rigid motions of the structure.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is no versioned release and no named checkpoint. The authors publish the data sets, the source code and a Colab notebook in one GitHub repository, whose default branch is colab and which was last pushed in November 2024. The paper computes four train and test splits, and the repository holds a single pickled model under predict/. A result must therefore name the commit, the split and the structure prediction settings rather than a checkpoint name. The repository declares no licence.

sections.title: What the authors report
sections.body: The model is small: 6,401 trained parameters. It was trained and tested on the data set of Inoue et al., 884 sequences, which the authors note is limited by how few measured absorption maxima exist. They report an average accuracy of 6.8 nm on the test set sequences, and in the abstract that more than half of the test sequences were predicted to within 0.03 eV after training on a balanced training set. Prediction of one structure takes seconds. These are the authors' own figures and have not been reproduced by Rewire.

notes: Points for a reviewer. Three naming and packaging facts. The repository is called OpsiGen, not RhoMax, and its README uses the OpsiGen name throughout; the paper calls the network RhoMax. Its default branch is colab, and there is no main or master branch, so the pinned commit a7f6ac3b is on that branch. No licence is declared for the code or for the pickled model in predict/, so both licence facts are not stated; the paper itself is CC BY 4.0, which covers the article and not the software. The context_length of 24 in the structured row is the size of the binding pocket the model reads, not a sequence length limit, and the parameter count of 6,401 is the paper's figure for the whole network. The local run instructions are written for the authors' cluster: the prediction script calls sbatch and activates a path under /cs/labs, so a reader will more likely want the Colab notebook, which was not read.
